fields.expected:
Most of what I've built ends up being a retrieval problem in disguise. For tSearch, I built a talent-discovery system that starts from seed candidates, expands through public GitHub and Substack collaboration graphs, scores heuristically, and only then runs rubric-driven LLM assessment. The hardest part was not the model. It was finding the right evidence in the first place, and keeping discovery separate from judgment so the LLM couldn't quietly paper over bad identity resolution. Search over the open web was consistently the weakest link.

So a company whose entire thesis is building real infrastructure for that, crawling the whole web, training embedding models over it, and building vector databases fast enough to serve it, is the part of the stack I actually want to work on. I also care about a question Exa sits close to: as AI makes generation cheap, judgment and evidence retrieval become the bottleneck. I spent the past year researching how institutions evaluate uncertain scientific work, and better search is a real part of that answer. I'd rather own a hard piece of infrastructure than ship demos.

fields.expected:
I built tSearch, a talent-discovery system based on the idea that someone's public work is a better signal of ability than their school or employer. It starts from named seed candidates and expands through public collaboration and publishing graphs like GitHub and Substack, then runs identity resolution, graph expansion, heuristic scoring, persistence, LLM assessment, and a recruiter digest. It's mostly TypeScript and Node with Playwright, Express, Vite, and OpenAI.

The part I'm proud of is the design decisions rather than the crawl. I kept discovery and assessment separate so the LLM judges can't silently correct an identity-resolution mistake or re-run discovery, and I didn't collapse the heuristic discovery score into the LLM assessment score. I also made missing evidence not count as negative evidence: if the system can't find enough public work to judge a dimension, it returns insufficient evidence instead of a low score. The judging is rubric-driven, with separate judges running in parallel and then synthesizing an evidence-cited assessment. I built the MVP fast and later talked through product direction with Cory Levy of Z Fellows.

fields.expected:
What keeps me building is a problem I've actually run into, and then getting the system in front of real users so I find out where I was wrong. I built ClarityAtlas end to end in Swift and SwiftUI, including a passive sleep-estimation system using HealthKit and Core Motion signals so users wouldn't need a wearable, and shipped it into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users. Getting there meant recruiting users, pitching, and explaining repeatedly why the thing should exist, which turned out to matter as much as the code.

The other thing that motivates me is retrieval and evaluation. At Intelehealth I designed an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard, and that convinced me generation is cheap while deciding whether an answer should be trusted is the hard part. That's why search interests me now: at Exa's scale, crawling the web, training embedding models, and building a vector database, the whole problem is surfacing the right evidence rather than just producing plausible text. I want to own a real piece of a system like that.
